Tell us about the property you lost to the 2022 demolition along the Lusada-Agbara Road. My property was demolished between February and March 2022 to make way for the road construction project from Agbara towards Atan. It comprised six shops and a three-bedroom flat. My wife’s Cherubim and Seraphim church was also located on the property, as she is a prophetess. I never imagined that a property I had worked so hard to acquire would one day be reduced to rubble. It represented years of hard work and investment, as well as the financial security I had hoped to enjoy in retirement. What is your professional background, and what informed your decision to invest in the property? I am a trained plastics engineer with a master’s degree. Over the years, I worked with several companies across northern, eastern and south-western Nigeria, including one of the country’s biggest plastics companies. I spent a significant part of my working life in the plastics industry before retiring. After retirement, I decided to settle in Atan, Ogun State, having spent most of my life in Lagos. I believed I had reached a stage where I could enjoy the fruits of my labour and live peacefully without the pressures of active employment. Acquiring the property was part of my plan for old age. I knew I would not remain in active employment forever, so I wanted something that would provide a steady income and prevent me from depending on my children or other people. The six shops were practically my lifeline and major source of income after retirement. I rented them out, and the proceeds helped me meet my daily needs. My wife also used one of the shops. Unfortunately, I was involved in an accident in 2012, which left me with a head injury and affected my eyesight. Although I received treatment, my condition gradually deteriorated. The rental income from the shops was particularly important because it helped me manage my needs despite my health challenges. I was not living an extravagant life; I only wanted to enjoy the comfort I had worked for. However, the demolition changed everything. It felt as though the years I had spent working and saving towards a comfortable retirement suddenly counted for nothing. Were you given prior notice before your property was demolished? Yes. We were given seven days’ notice before the demolition. Although we knew it was going to happen, receiving a notice did not mean we were prepared for the consequences or had alternative accommodation. What assurances were you given about compensation before the demolition? We were told that we would be compensated. The authorities asked us to submit our property documents and take photographs of our buildings. Those who had relevant documents were instructed to provide them as part of the process. I had several documents relating to my property, and my wife also took photographs of the structures. We complied because we believed the government would fulfil its promise and that the documentation was the first step towards receiving compensation. However, nobody told us exactly how much we would receive or when payment would be made. We held on to the assurance that the government would not leave us stranded after taking our properties. What happened to your wife’s church after the demolition? It was where my wife carried out her religious activities and where members gathered to worship. It occupied about half a plot, while our residential building stood on a full plot. Losing it was another painful experience for our family. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources Before the demolition, the church was a properly constructed building with plastered and painted walls and a POP ceiling. Today, members gather to worship under a temporary canopy because we cannot afford to rebuild. We are grateful to those who have supported us, but it is painful to see how much we have lost. Where did you move to after losing your property? For two years, I had to stay with a friend who was also a landlord. It was not an easy experience, especially at my age. I worked for years and owned my property, yet I suddenly found myself depending on another person for accommodation. I now live in Odugbemi, Atan, about a 10-minute drive from Atan. My children managed to put up another two-bedroom flat for me. However, the building is still uncompleted. It has not been plastered, there is no ceiling, and there are no doors. It is simply a place I can enter and stay. I sleep on the floor. Although I am grateful to my children for providing somewhere for me to stay, the building is far from being a comfortable home. Imagine someone who once owned six shops and a three-bedroom flat now living in an uncompleted building without basic facilities. I never thought I would find myself in this situation after spending so many years working and investing. How has the loss of your rental income affected your daily survival? Since the demolition, I have lost the regular income I depended on to meet my basic needs. Before then, the shops provided money for feeding and other expenses. I was financially independent and did not have to rely on anyone to take care of myself. Since losing the property, however, I have depended largely on financial assistance from some of my old classmates. Without their support, I honestly do not know how I would have survived. It is difficult for someone who spent most of his life working and taking responsibility for himself to suddenly become dependent on others. Even feeding has become a struggle, and I sometimes have to wait for assistance before I can meet my basic needs. How has the demolition compounded your health challenges and affected your ability to seek treatment? Unfortunately, my eyesight has deteriorated to the point where I can barely see, and I have been unable to afford further treatment. Everyday activities that I once performed independently have become difficult, and I now depend on others for assistance. My children have been doing their best to support me, but their resources are limited. The little money they managed to raise went into building the uncompleted house where I now live. They wanted to ensure I had somewhere to stay after spending two years with a friend. Unfortunately, this has left very little for my medical needs. I cannot afford the further treatment my eyes require, even though my condition continues to affect my daily activities. My deteriorating health has also limited my ability to participate in the activities of other affected property owners seeking compensation. I can no longer easily join them at meetings, write letters or engage with the authorities. It is frustrating that, having lost my property, I am also physically constrained from actively pursuing the compensation we were promised. It is painful because I know I need medical attention but cannot afford it. My children have their own responsibilities, and I do not want to put more pressure on them. I want to regain my independence and take care of myself without having to depend on others for my basic needs. What response have you received from the authorities since submitting your documents? We have not received the response we expected. I heard that some affected property owners had written to the government, explaining their situation and demanding the promised compensation, but there had been no response. We also heard that people whose properties were demolished in other locations were compensated and that their cases had been settled. This makes it difficult to understand why our situation remains unresolved. We submitted the requested documents and have waited for years without any meaningful outcome. We are not asking for something that was never discussed. We were promised compensation, and we simply want the government to fulfil that promise. What steps have you personally taken to secure the compensation? I have made several formal attempts to get the government’s attention. I personally submitted letters to the Governor’s Office and the Federal Ministry of Works, among other relevant offices. I still have copies of the letters and acknowledgement receipts showing that they were received. Despite these efforts, nothing has been done. What prompted the affected property owners to embark on the recent protest? We agreed to allow the government to carry out the project because we were assured that we would be compensated. However, several years later, nothing has been paid to us. We have written several letters to different government offices, including the Governor’s Office and the Federal Ministry of Works, but we have received no response. We decided to protest to draw attention to our plight and ensure that our complaints reach the appropriate authorities, including the President. How has the prolonged wait for compensation affected other property owners? It has been a very difficult experience. Some of the affected property owners have died, while others are seriously ill and bedridden. I remember one landlord who personally appealed to the governor to help us, but he died about a year later. Many people depended on their properties for survival. Some had shops and businesses there, while others relied on rental income for their upkeep. The demolition took away their means of livelihood, and some are still struggling to recover from the losses. We understand that some property owners whose buildings were demolished in other areas between 2024 and 2025 have received compensation, with some reportedly paid substantial amounts. Those affected along the Atan-to-Sokoto axis were compensated, but a section of the area, particularly those of us along the Agbara Road axis, was left out. Why were we excluded? We have also heard that some affected property owners received compensation as recently as two or three months ago, yet we are still waiting. Why are those of us affected along the Atan-Lusada-Agbara axis still being left out? We complied with the instructions given to us and simply want the government to fulfil its promise without further delay. What has been the hardest part of adjusting to life after the demolition? The hardest part is having to live with the reality that everything I worked for is gone while my health continues to deteriorate. I lost my property, rental income and the financial independence I had built over the years. At the same time, I am struggling with my eyesight and cannot afford the treatment I need. It is difficult to accept that I have gone from being a property owner with six shops and a three-bedroom flat to someone who depends on friends for financial assistance and sleeps on the floor in an uncompleted building. Some of the other affected landlords have also suffered. Some have become tenants after losing their properties, while others have died. These were people who invested their savings and years of hard work in properties they believed would provide security for themselves and their families. I acquired the property so that I would not become a burden to anyone in my old age. Yet, I now depend on others for things I once provided for myself. I am not asking to live a luxurious life. I only want to regain some dignity, receive the compensation we were promised and have the opportunity to take care of my health. What exactly do you want the Federal Government to do after years of waiting? We are not looking for trouble or interested in violence. All we want is our compensation. We want the government to fulfil the promise made to us and pay us what we are entitled to. Some of us invested years of hard work and savings in those properties. In my case, the six shops were my source of income after retirement. Losing them has left me in a difficult situation, particularly as I am also battling serious health challenges. I want the government to understand that behind every demolished property is a human being and a family whose lives have been affected. These were not just buildings that were pulled down. People lost their homes, businesses, sources of income and the security they had worked towards in old age. How much longer are we expected to wait? We submitted our documents, complied with the instructions given to us and have waited for years. We simply want the government to honour its promise. We do not want confrontation or violence. We want justice and the opportunity to rebuild our lives with the compensation we are entitled to. Temitope Adetunji Temitope Adetunji is a journalist at Punch Newspapers who specialises in human-interest storytelling. She brings years of experience in online journalism into her work, having transitioned into print reporting with a strong digital foundation. Temitope is passionate about amplifying real-life narratives and highlighting the lived experiences that shape everyday people. Her reporting reflects hands-on newsroom experience, empathy-driven storytelling, and a commitment to accurate, people-centred journalism.
